chapters.title: Chapter 3: Risk, Returns and the Power Law

lessons.title: Getting Your Money Out: Acquisitions, Secondary Sales and IPOs

children.text: In May 2018, Walmart agreed to pay $16 billion for 77% of Flipkart, valuing the company at about $20.8 billion. Accel and Tiger Global had backed Flipkart more than eight years earlier, when it was reportedly valued at around $50 million. That is what an exit looks like: the moment someone finally pays cash for shares that were, until then, just numbers on a cap table. Unlisted startup shares cannot be sold on NSE or BSE, so every rupee of paper gain in the last two lessons depends on an exit actually happening. This lesson covers the ways out, how long they take, the rules that lock you in, and the traps that can shrink what you receive.

body.text: A startup investment becomes money only when someone else pays for your shares. Until then, every valuation is a number on a slide. Understand how you will get out before you decide to get in.

children.text: The Four Ways Out

body.caption: How angel investments end (timings are typical, not guaranteed)

cells: Another company or a PE fund buys the whole startup
The acquirer, in cash, shares or both
Often 3 to 10 years after your investment
Low: the board and major shareholders decide
You sell some or all of your shares to another investor or back to the company
A new investor, fund or the company itself
Possible at any time, most often alongside a later funding round
Medium: you can try, but you need a buyer and often other shareholders' consent
The company lists on NSE and BSE, and your shares become tradable after a lock-in
Often 8 to 12 years or more, for a small minority of companies
Low: the company decides when to list
The company closes and creditors are paid first
Any time, most often in the first few years

children.text: Acquisitions: When Someone Buys the Whole Company

markDefs.definition: A small acquisition where the buyer mainly wants the startup's team, not its product or revenue. Investors often receive little or nothing.
A shareholders' agreement clause that lets a required majority force all shareholders, including small angels, to sell on the same terms if they approve a sale.
A clause that lets minority shareholders join a sale by a major shareholder on the same terms, so they are not left behind.

children.text: Acquisitions are the most common positive exit for startups. They range from blockbuster deals like Flipkart to small
acqui-hires
that barely return investors' money. As an angel, you rarely get a vote that matters. If the founders and larger investors approve a sale, a
drag-along right
can require you to sell too. The protection that works in your favour is a
tag-along right
, which lets you join if a major shareholder sells.

markDefs.definition: Part of the sale price held back by a third party for a set period to cover claims such as undisclosed liabilities, and released later if no claims arise.
Part of the sale price paid only if the business hits agreed targets after the acquisition.

children.text: The headline price is also not what lands in your bank account on day one. Buyers commonly hold back part of the price in
escrow
and tie another part to future performance through an
earn-out
. Liquidation preferences, covered in Chapter 2, come off the top before common shareholders share the rest.

body.caption: A ₹200 crore acquisition, and your 0.5% stake (illustrative, ignoring liquidation preferences)

cells: Over 2 years, only if targets are met

body.title: What arrives at closing?
body.prompt: A logistics company buys a startup for ₹300 crore. 60% is paid upfront, 10% goes into escrow and 30% is an earn-out. You own 0.4% and there are no liquidation preferences. How much cash do you receive at closing, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: Your headline share is 0.4% × ₹300 crore = ₹1.2 crore. Upfront is 60% of that: ₹72 lakh. Another ₹12 lakh sits in escrow, and up to ₹36 lakh depends on the earn-out. If targets are missed, your total could be ₹84 lakh, not ₹1.2 crore.

body.title: Paid in cash vs paid in the acquirer's shares

columns.label: Cash deal
points: Your return is locked in at closing, apart from escrow and earn-outs
No further exposure to the buyer's fortunes
Simple to value and plan around
Tax is typically due in the year you receive the money

columns.label: Share-swap deal
points: You swap one set of shares for another
If the acquirer is unlisted, you may still have no way to sell
Your final return depends on how the acquirer performs
Upside if the acquirer grows, but a second round of the same exit problem

children.text: Secondary Sales: Selling Before the Finish Line

markDefs.definition: A clause giving the company or existing shareholders the right to buy your shares on the same terms before you can sell them to an outsider.

children.text: A secondary sale is the one exit you can actively pursue yourself. The most common opportunity comes during a large later funding round, when an incoming investor wants a bigger stake than the company is issuing and agrees to buy some existing shares from early holders. Companies also sometimes buy back shares, often to give employees liquidity on their stock options. Expect two frictions. Buyers usually demand a discount to the latest round price, and your shareholders' agreement will likely include a
right of first refusal
, so you cannot simply sell to anyone you like.

body.title: Selling at a discount
body.prompt: You hold 1,250 KhetSetu shares, bought at ₹800 each for ₹10 lakh. KhetSetu's latest round was priced at ₹2,000 per share. A fund offers to buy your shares at a 25% discount to that price. How much would you receive, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: Discounted price = ₹2,000 × 0.75 = ₹1,500 per share. 1,250 × ₹1,500 = ₹18,75,000, or ₹18.75 lakh. That is 1.875x your money in hand today, compared with ₹25 lakh on paper at the round price. Whether the discount is worth it depends on how confident you are in a bigger future exit.

body.text: Be careful with websites and apps that trade "unlisted" or "pre-IPO" shares. SEBI has repeatedly warned investors, including in a December 2024 press release and again in June 2026, that such platforms are not recognised by SEBI and that trades on them fall outside the investor protection framework of SEBI and the stock exchanges. Stock brokers are allowed to deal only on recognised exchanges. Prices on these platforms can be far from fair value, and you have little recourse if something goes wrong.

children.text: IPOs: The Long Road to NSE and BSE

markDefs.definition: The part of an IPO in which existing shareholders sell their shares to the public. The money goes to the sellers, not to the company.
A period after an IPO during which pre-IPO shareholders cannot sell their shares.

children.text: An IPO is the rarest and usually the largest exit. Existing investors can exit in two ways: by selling in the IPO itself through an
offer for sale
, or by selling on the exchange after the
lock-in

ends. Urban Company's IPO in September 2025 shows the mix. The ₹1,900 crore issue, with a price band of ₹98 to ₹103 per share, included ₹472 crore of fresh shares for the company and ₹1,428 crore of offer for sale, with early backers such as Accel, Bessemer and Elevation Capital among the sellers.

stats.label: Of which offer for sale
stats.context: About 75% of the issue went to selling shareholders

stats.label: Lock-in for non-promoter pre-IPO shares
stats.context: From IPO allotment on the main board; 1 year on the SME platform

stats.label: Lock-in for promoters' minimum contribution
stats.context: Reduced from 3 years by SEBI's August 2021 amendment

body.label: When most angels can actually sell after an IPO
body.context: Under SEBI's ICDR Regulations, non-promoter pre-issue shares on the main board are generally locked in for 6 months from allotment, subject to certain exemptions. Your shares still carry market risk during that period.

body.text: A strong listing day does not guarantee a strong exit for pre-IPO holders. When the lock-in ends, many early investors become free to sell at the same time, which can weigh on the share price. Angels who plan to sell in stages after the lock-in, rather than all at once, reduce the risk of selling at a single bad moment.

body.title: A typical successful angel exit path (illustrative)

events.title: You invest
events.description: ₹10 lakh into a pre-seed or seed round. No way to sell.

events.title: Seed to Series B
events.description: Paper value may rise, but shares remain illiquid. Most companies that fail do so here.

events.title: Lock-in ends

children.text: A Quick Word on Tax at Exit

How your gain is taxed depends on whether the shares are listed or unlisted when you sell, and how long you held them. For unlisted shares sold on or after 23 July 2024, a holding period of more than 24 months makes the gain long-term, taxed at 12.5% without indexation; shorter holdings are taxed at your slab rate. Listed shares follow different rules. Chapter 4 covers angel taxation properly, including how the rules apply when shares you bought unlisted are later sold on an exchange.

body.title: The exit you control
body.question: Which exit route can an individual angel most realistically start on their own initiative?
options: An IPO on NSE and BSE
An acquisition of the whole company
A secondary sale of their own shares, subject to the shareholders' agreement
Forcing the company to buy back all investor shares
body.explanation: IPOs and acquisitions are decided by the company, its board and major shareholders. An angel can look for a buyer for their own shares, although a right of first refusal, transfer restrictions and discounts may apply. Companies are generally not obliged to buy back an angel's shares on demand.

body.title: Tanvi's acquisition offer
body.scenario: Tanvi, an angel in Bengaluru, owns 0.3% of a SaaS startup. A larger unlisted software company offers to buy the whole startup for ₹400 crore: 60% in cash at closing and 40% in the acquirer's own shares. The board and the lead VC support the deal, and the shareholders' agreement has a drag-along clause. Tanvi believes that if the startup stayed independent, it could list on NSE and BSE in about four years at a ₹1,500 crore valuation, by which time she expects to be diluted to 0.25%.
body.prompt: What is the offer worth to Tanvi, how does it compare with her IPO hope, and what should she do?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The offer: 0.3% × ₹400 crore = ₹1.2 crore headline, before any liquidation preferences. That is ₹72 lakh in cash and ₹48 lakh in unlisted shares of the acquirer, which she may not be able to sell for years.
2. The IPO hope: 0.25% × ₹1,500 crore = ₹3.75 crore on paper, but only if the company survives, grows as planned, actually lists in four years and the market is receptive, plus a 6-month lock-in before she can sell.
3. She may not have a real choice. With board support, the lead VC in favour and a drag-along clause, she can likely be required to sell on the same terms.
4. What she should do: ask for the full payout waterfall showing liquidation preferences, confirm her exact cash amount, understand the acquirer's shares (valuation, rights, any path to liquidity), check for escrow or earn-outs, and get tax advice on the cash and share components.
5. The lesson: a certain ₹72 lakh in cash today can be worth more than a much larger but uncertain number years away, and for small angels, the decision is often made by others.

body.title: Name the IPO component
body.textWithBlank: The part of an IPO in which existing shareholders sell their shares to the public is called an offer for ___.
body.explanation: In an offer for sale, the money goes to the selling shareholders, not to the company. In Urban Company's IPO, about ₹1,428 crore of the ₹1,900 crore issue was offer for sale.

cards.definition: A small acquisition mainly for the startup's team; investors often receive little or nothing.
Lets the required majority force all shareholders to sell on the same terms in an approved sale.
Lets minority shareholders join a sale by a major shareholder on the same terms.
Part of the sale price held back for a period to cover claims, released later if none arise.
Part of the sale price paid only if the business hits agreed targets after the deal.
The company or existing shareholders can buy your shares on the same terms before an outsider can.
The part of an IPO where existing shareholders sell shares to the public; proceeds go to the sellers.
A period after an IPO when pre-IPO shareholders cannot sell; 6 months for non-promoters on the main board.

points: Unlisted shares turn into money only through an acquisition, a secondary sale or an IPO; a shutdown usually returns nothing.
Acquisitions are the most common positive exit, but drag-along clauses mean small angels rarely control the decision.
The headline acquisition price shrinks through liquidation preferences, escrow, earn-outs and share-swap components.
Secondary sales are the one exit you can pursue yourself, usually at a discount and subject to rights of first refusal.
IPOs are rare and slow; pre-IPO shares of non-promoters on the main board are generally locked in for 6 months after allotment.
Avoid unregistered unlisted-share platforms, which SEBI has repeatedly warned fall outside investor protection.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or tax advice. Lock-in rules have exemptions, and tax rules depend on your circumstances and may change. Deal figures for real companies are based on public reports. KhetSetu, Tanvi and all illustrative numbers are hypothetical. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a qualified tax professional before acting.
